Property sales that complete on this day have a lower median price. Air fares are cheaper. Weddings are non-existent. And motor collisions increase. How did it become so mired in superstition?
“I have only worked one Friday 13th wedding in my 14 years in business,” says Caroline Smyth, a photographer and celebrant based in Larne, Northern Ireland. “I definitely think it is down to the fact that it’s a date surrounded by superstition. People are maybe afraid it’s a bad omen for their marriage.”
Smyth’s sole Friday 13th wedding, in September 2013, was the first she ever photographed – and it kickstarted her career. But for many businesses, the date is not so auspicious. From weddings to flights, job interviews to elective surgeries, many people avoid booking anything of significance on this date, believing it to be bad luck.
Today is the third Friday 13th in 2026 – the maximum number of times this date can occur in any year in the Gregorian calendar, and the only such year this decade. The last year with three Friday 13ths was 2015. But where does western wariness of this date come from – and is there any evidence that it does bring bad luck?
The origins of the superstition are not entirely clear. Some believe the number 13 to be unlucky in itself, thanks to a mix of religious, folkloric and cultural traditions. In Norse mythology, for example, triskaidekaphobia – fear or avoidance of the number 13 – can be traced back to the story of Loki , a “trickster” or god of mischief, who crashed a banquet in Valhalla, becoming the 13th guest and then murdering the host’s popular servant, Fimafeng.
In Christianity, there is also the idea that Judas, the disciple who betrayed Jesus, was the 13th to sit at the table for the Last Supper , with Jesus’s crucifixion the following day (and which is itself believed to have taken place on a Friday).
Others attribute Friday 13th’s supposed bad luck to the Knights Templar, hundreds of whom were arrested for heresy on Friday 13 October 1307 . items.title: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback
items.desc: Long thought to have been looted from northern England by Scottish tribes, the larger-than-life leg may have actually been displayed in Roman Scotland, before it was carefully dismantled and buried by retreating forces
items.text:
In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes.
But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops.
“This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement .
Roman campaigns into modern-day Scotland began in the 70s C.E., several decades after the conquest of Britain . Emperor Hadrian , who ruled from 117 C.E. to 138 C.E., consolidated the Romans’ northernmost limit in northern England, where Hadrian’s Wall still stands.
Hadrian’s successor, Antoninus Pius, pushed his armies north again, and in the early 140s C.E. fortified a position about 100 miles north of Hadrian’s Wall, known as the Antonine Wall . A few years after Antoninus Pius died in 161 C.E., the Roman armies retreated south, back to Hadrian’s Wall.
The timeline of the second century C.E. Roman invasion of southern Scotland—and eventual withdrawal—provides the context for the bronze limb.
Close inspection reveals that rather than bearing jagged axe or saw marks, the upper edge remains intact, just as Roman metalworkers originally cast it in the 140s C.E. An absence of gilding around the knee indicates that the leg was covered by a tunic or cloak, part of a larger statue, perhaps similar to the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome
“When you look, you see it hasn’t been hacked off, it’s a complete leg,” Hunter explains to the Telegraph ’s Ruby Cline. “So rather than loot, it looks as if the statue has been carefully decommissioned at the end of its life.”
When Roman forces abandoned southern Scotland, they routinely dismantled and buried prized monuments, including stone altars and inscriptions from the Antonine Wall, rather than leave them behind, per the statement.

Bad parking can feel surprisingly personal because it breaks an unspoken agreement people have when sharing public spaces. According to Drive , drivers generally expect everyone to use available parking fairly and avoid making others deal with the consequences of their carelessness.
Someone who parks across two spaces, blocks another vehicle, or leaves their car at an awkward angle may seem to be prioritizing their own convenience over everyone else's. This can create more frustration than the parking mistake itself, particularly when other people are left struggling to find a spot or get where they need to go.
Part of this reaction also comes from how people perceive territory and personal space. Even though parking bays are public , drivers can become possessive of a space they believe they have a right to use. Cars can also feel like extensions of their owners, which explains why finding another vehicle parked too close or carelessly beside yours can feel like an intrusion.
The frustration can become even greater when someone is already running late, looking for a parking spot, or trying to get somewhere important. Interestingly, parking lines make these disagreements particularly easy to recognize because they establish clear visual boundaries. Unlike many social expectations, there is little ambiguity about whether a car is occupying more space than it should.
These expectations are part of a much broader set of unwritten rules governing how people share public spaces. Spacing explores how everyday etiquette largely comes down to recognizing that strangers have needs too, whether that means keeping doorways clear, allowing people to move freely, or avoiding unnecessary inconvenience.
Parking follows the same principle: people should take only the space they need and leave the rest available to others. Similar courtesies apply in everyday situations, such as not placing a bag on a seat someone else could use, moving aside when stopping on a busy pavement, and waiting your turn instead of pushing ahead in a queue.
Following these small social conventions helps make communal areas more comfortable and prevents unnecessary disagreements. items.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
items.desc: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.
items.text:
Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.
Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.
Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.
"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.
Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people
Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says. , external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

items.title: German Renaissance Master Albrecht Altdorfer Pioneered Landscape Painting. A Work Previously Unknown to Scholars Just Emerged After 70 Years in a Private Collection
items.desc: Painted around 1520, the newly identified painting is one of only three pure landscapes painted in oil by the artist. It depicts a lush forest scene with castle ruins and a rainbow emerging from stormy skies
items.text:
For nearly seven decades, a small 16th-century painting of a forest hung in a private collection in Switzerland, unbeknownst to art historians. Now, the 500-year-old work has emerged into the limelight, newly attributed to Albrecht Altdorfer , a German Renaissance artist who pioneered landscape painting.
Measuring roughly nine inches long by eight inches wide and dating from around 1520, A Thickly Wooded Landscape With a Rainbow Behind the Trees and a Distant Outcrop to the Right Beneath a Cloud-Laden Sky will head to auction at Sotheby’s in London on December 9.
“Every inch of this intimate picture is imbued with an intense mood that transcends its scale … It somehow still feels as modern and immediate as it would have appeared to those seeing it when it was first painted,” George Gordon , co-chair of Sotheby’s Old Masters department, says in a statement . “To add to the known body of work of one of the great masters of the Northern Renaissance is one of the most exciting discoveries imaginable in our field.”
The painting, which does not appear in Altdorfer’s catalogue raisonné and was only identified earlier this year, is expected to sell for up to $6.6 million. “We don’t really know what it’s worth because it’s many decades since an Altdorfer last came to the market,” Gordon tells the Art Newspaper ’s Catherine Hickley. “It could fetch more than our estimate.”
Until its discovery, scholars knew of just two oil landscapes by Altdorfer, both held in major European museums: Landscape With a Footbridge at London’s National Gallery and Landscape of the Danube Near Regensburg at Munich’s Alte Pinakothek . No Altdorfer painting has appeared on the market since 1980, when the National Gallery acquired Christ Taking Leave of His Mother .
Painted in oil on vellum, A Thickly Wooded Landscape is the smallest and most densely forested of Altdorfer’s surviving landscapes in any medium, including engravings, etchings and drawings. In the foreground, tangled evergreens and mossy undergrowth rise without a single human figure in sight, while a distant castle perches atop a rocky outcrop on the right. Overhead, heavy clouds part just enough to reveal a faint glow from the sun, whose light catches a delicate rainbow arching behind the trees.

items.text:
A viral moment from a doorbell camera that reached millions of people has now raised more than $76,000 to support a woman who spends her days caring for others.
When Suzanna Metcalf arrived at Pastor Neal Seiwert’s home in Castle Rock, Colorado last year, she apologized as she had mixed up their pizza order, and would have to return with the correct order. She blamed “getting old,” but the struggle on her face was clear.
Metcalf works delivery shifts while serving as the full-time caregiver for her 82-year-old mother, managing daily care, medical needs and household expenses.
Instead of frustration, Seiwert, his wife Hailee, and their three young daughters stepped outside, placed their hands on her shoulders, and prayed for her. The short clip, captured by a doorbell camera, showed Metcalf visibly moved by the unexpected kindness after a long day of work.
The video, posted by Seiwert, quickly went viral, with hundreds of commenters, who almost all had the same question: How can we help?
The Seiwerts found Metcalf, and with her permission, started a GoFundMe, which describes Suzanna as a woman who has spent years putting others first.
What began as a modest effort quickly grew. More than 2,600 donors have contributed over the last year, raising over $76,000 — far exceeding the initial $10,000 goal— to give Suzanna some financial breathing room as she continues caring for her mom.
Seiwert told the New York Post he wanted Metcalf to feel both his family’s support and a broader sense of being valued. “So many people are commenting on how it brought them to tears. There are many people who simply just need love,” he said.
A viral moment doesn’t change the demands of caregiving and delivery work. But it has shown, in concrete form, that one small pause for kindness can open the door for real help.

items.title: More Than 3,000 Tarantulas Were Found Hidden in Socks During a Major Wildlife Trafficking Bust at an Airport in Lima, Peru
items.desc: According to Peruvian officials, the three European travelers—including one who's been identified as a "renowned tarantula researcher"—could have made around $1.68 million from the creepy-crawly loot
items.text:
Authorities in Peru say they have foiled a plot to smuggle more than 3,000 tarantulas—including species not yet described in scientific publications—out of the country.
After receiving an anonymous tip , officials intercepted three travelers—two German citizens and one Polish citizen—at Jorge Chávez International Airport in Lima as they were checking in at the boarding area. When they searched the travelers’ luggage, they found thousands of eggs, hatchlings and adult spiders hidden in socks, according to a November 4 statement from the National Forest and Wildlife Service of Peru (SERFOR).
“We noticed that some of them were moving,” Cora Suárez , a SERFOR forest and wildlife control technician who works at the airport, tells the Agence France-Presse . “There were small ones and large ones.”
Workers used slender wooden sticks to gently brush the spiders into clear plastic containers. Once officials are done investigating them, the tarantulas will be taken to an authorized breeding center.
The travelers were trying to fly to Germany. Instead, they were detained by the Peruvian National Police’s environmental crimes unit and now face criminal charges.
Officials have not released the names of the individuals. However, one of the travelers was a “renowned tarantula researcher,” according to the statement, per a translation by the New York Times ’ Amanda Holpuch.
Authorities suspect the individuals were smuggling the spiders for private collections, research and the exotic pet trade. Suárez tells the AFP that one tarantula can sell for roughly $560 in Europe, meaning the smugglers could have made around $1.68 million from the more than 3,000 tarantulas they had hidden in their suitcases.
The spiders originated from several different parts of Peru, including the cities of Cajamarca, Cusco and Junín, and the regions of La Libertad and Loreto. Officials are still trying to pinpoint all the species in the loot but said it included several brightly colored creatures.
Wildlife trafficking is the world’s fourth-largest form of organized crime, with an estimated annual value of up to $20 billion .

items.title: What could El Niño mean for winter weather in the US and Canada?
items.desc: El Niño winters typically bring more rain in the southern USA and drier, warmer conditions further north but the impacts on snowfall are complex.
items.text:
Montreal, Canada was badly hit by the Great Ice Storm of 1998 which was blamed, in part, on El Niño.
The developing El Niño - already the strongest on record by some measures - continues to grow and could have profound effects on the weather across North America this autumn and winter.
The naturally-occurring climate phenomenon sees trade winds over the Pacific Ocean, which usually blow from east to west, weakening or reversing with warm water instead spreading eastwards.
This releases heat into the atmosphere which can drive major shifts in global weather patterns.
Impacts in the US and Canada are varied, with a greater chance of a warm and dry winter in northern areas and more risk of flooding rain further south.
There is also some evidence that El Niño can increase the likelihood of disruption to the stratospheric polar vortex which can, in turn, bring snowfall later in winter.
No two El Niños are the same and the impacts are not guaranteed - the odds are just shifted in favour of certain outcomes.

The eastward shift of warm ocean waters associated with El Niño can cause the Pacific jet stream to move south and extend eastwards, directing rain-bearing weather systems across the southern USA.
This typically leads to wetter winters during El Niño years.
The likely impacts of El Niño on winter weather vary across different parts of North America.
The latest three month forecast , external from the US National Weather Service (NWS) suggests this is a likely outcome for the winter of 2026-2027.
South-eastern states, including Florida, Georgia and the Carolinas, have the greatest chance of seeing above-average rainfall.
The El Niño winter of 1997-1998 brought significant flooding in the south-east and spun up tornadoes for Florida.
Severe flooding hit Long Beach, California in February 2024.
California could well find itself in the firing line with forecasts suggesting a wet winter is likely.
Governor Gavin Newsom has already declared a state of emergency , external ahead of anticipated floods and mudslides.
Areas scarred by recent wildfires are particularly susceptible, with the effects of climate change exacerbating the risks.
Many past El Niños have been wet here, with winter 2023-2024 bringing relief from drought. However this is not always the case. In the strong El Niño of 2015-2016, California actually had below-average rainfall.

items.text:
The world’s largest demonstration plant for a new kind of renewable energy storage is up and running in the west of the China.
Called liquid-air energy storage (LAES) the plant uses renewable electricity to compress air to extreme densities until it turns to liquid. It can then be rapidly released to power a turbine and discharge that green energy back into the grid.
China has received numerous plaudits for its rapid adoption of renewable energy at both scale and speed, and this new facility in Qinghai Province brings in a key missing element to the renewable build-out: grid-scale battery storage for when the Sun isn’t shining and the wind isn’t blowing.
Not that either of those happen very often in Qinghai, which encompasses parts of the Tibetan Plateau, and Mongolia-like grasslands and desert, where both sun and wind are famously relentless.
Described as “the world’s largest grid-connected liquid-air energy storage facility by both rated power and energy capacity,” the facility is rated at 600 megawatt-hours, and will substantially back up the renewable contribution to the regional power grid by providing 10 hours of continual power supply when necessary. Additionally, it was built with its own solar farm, rated at 250MW.
LAES works by turning ordinary air into a liquid, keeping that liquid in insulated tanks, and then converting it back into electricity when needed.
When electricity is plentiful, it powers machinery that draws in air, compresses it and cools it to extremely low temperatures of around -190°C. At this point, the air becomes a liquid, taking up far less space than it did as a gas.
When power is needed, the liquid air is pumped to high pressure and warmed. As it warms, it rapidly expands back into a gas and can be used to spin a turbine connected to an electricity generator, sending power back to the grid.
A cool party trick is how the system utilizes the excess heat and cold: it stores both for heating and cooling the air as needed, reducing energy consumption and environmental disturbance.

items.text:
On Sunday, November 8, hundreds of people gathered around Chicago’s iconic Cloud Gate sculpture (aka “The Bean”) with one unusual goal: moving it 7 inches to the left. It was quite an ambitious feat, considering the sculpture weighs about 110 tons. Although the crowd was ultimately unsuccessful, the humorous stunt brought Chicagoans together for an afternoon of fun.
The event began with flyers posted around Chicago that simply read, “We need to move the bean seven inches to the left,” with no further explanation. The flyers instructed people to gather at Millennium Park at exactly 12:47 p.m., and the unusual request quickly gained attention on social media.
The reason behind the stunt was an ongoing internet joke that claims a man is trapped inside the sculpture. According to an online invitation for the event, moving The Bean would supposedly reveal a hidden door, allowing people to give the imaginary man a pickle and other resources.
On the day of the event, hundreds of people showed up to participate, with videos showing crowds pushing against the sculpture in unison. Despite their combined efforts, The Bean didn’t budge.
Created by artist Anish Kapoor between 2004 and 2006, The Bean’s nickname comes from the sculpture’s unusual shape. Its 168 stainless steel plates are welded together and polished to create a seamless, mirror-like surface perfect for pictures and selfies. Over the years, it has become one of Chicago’s most recognizable landmarks.
Although the crowd couldn’t accomplish its original goal, the Millennium Park Foundation welcomed the playful gathering. Kathryn Deery, an executive director for the foundation, told People that the event was a creative way to bring people together and celebrate one of the city’s most famous landmarks.
The sculpture remained in place and received its usual cleaning afterward, leaving behind little more than extra handprints and a memorable afternoon for the people who participated.

items.title: The Handwritten Final Draft of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' Speech Was Considered Lost. It Turned Out to Be Sitting in a Desk Drawer for Decades
items.desc: Across seven yellow notepad pages, King is seen wrestling with word choice and revising his remarks the night before the March on Washington. The manuscript will head to auction in January and is expected to pull in more than $10 million
items.text:
It was late on August 27, 1963, and Martin Luther King Jr. was huddled with a group of his closest advisors in the lobby of the Willard Hotel in Washington, D.C.
They were drafting King’s closing remarks for the March on Washington , officially the March on Washington for Jobs and Freedom, which was set to start in just 12 hours. The group went back and forth on the message: Should it be ideological or Biblical? Directed towards the students marching or the nation at large?
As the night wore on, King eventually bowed out. “Okay brothers,” Clarence B. Jones , an activist and speechwriter for King, recalled him saying. “Thank you so much everybody for your suggestions and input … I am now going upstairs to my room to counsel with my Lord.”
Alone in his suite, King stayed up until 4 a.m., writing and revising his remarks on a yellow notepad, scratching out swaths of text in blue ink. He then sent these marked-up pages to be typed, forming the basis of his canonical “I Have a Dream” speech , delivered to more than 250,000 demonstrators gathered by the Lincoln Memorial .
Scholars have long assumed that the original, handwritten final draft had been discarded amid the day’s chaos. But six decades later, the manuscript has resurfaced from a drawer of one of King’s former aides. The seven yellow pages are set to be auctioned at Christie’s in January, where the draft is expected to sell for more than $10 million.
“When I first saw these pages and realized what they were, I was astounded,” Christie’s manuscripts specialist Peter Klarnet says in a statement . “This is a treasure of American history … Reading along, you’re there in the moment with Dr. King, watching him compose it and making edits in real time.”
Civil rights leader and philanthropist Xernona Clayton found the pages in the late 1990s. They were tucked in an envelope labeled “speech,” nestled among other papers in a desk drawer belonging to her late husband, Edward , one of King’s aides and speechwriters.
Clayton knew it was an important document related to the “I Have a Dream” speech but not that it was the final manuscript. She tucked it back in the desk drawer, not wanting to disrespect King’s memory by selling or displaying his memorabilia.
But in recent years, she changed her mind. “Now that I’m older, I’m wiser,” Clayton, now 96, tells the New York Times ’ Jennifer Schuessler. “It just seems like something that important ought to be shared.”

items.text:
Some people (the lucky ones!) instinctively know how to make others laugh. Others take a more academic approach to comedy, humor, and laughter.
No matter which of these categories you fall into, the fact is that you can learn to amuse and entertain other people. This requires understanding the psychology of humor. And that means getting to grips with incongruity .
The American Psychological Association emphasizes that, according to research, incongruity is the key ingredient in getting others to laugh. Another vital factor is uncovering an unspoken truth.
Topher Bellavia, a member of the Washington Improv Theater, points out that creating successful scenes means mirroring the world in a slightly askew way.
Showing the world from a slightly different perspective means leaning into absurdity and exaggeration.
“Our basic mantra is 'truth in comedy.' People want to see themselves on stage, and they want to see people they know on stage. When they see that, it resonates with them and it causes them, for some reason, to laugh,” Bellavia told the APA.
And yet, improv pros and comedians aren’t always sure why they make others laugh. It sometimes comes as a surprise to them, too.
“As a performer, [audience laughter] can be very disorienting. Sometimes I'll do something that I don't even intend to be funny, and it will be hysterical to someone,” another member of the Washington Improv Theater, Anna Trester, said.
Never miss a story that brings joy to the world. Add us on Google
According to researcher and psychology professor Rod Martin, PhD, at the University of Western Ontario, incongruity, an idea or object being out of place, lies at the heart of humor.
Furthermore, the juxtaposition of truth and incongruity provides the audience with different perspectives on situations that they find familiar.
In a nutshell, humor helps you see the familiar in a fresh, new way by focusing on a mismatch between your expectations and reality.
However, what’s also needed is a playful atmosphere where there’s no threat.
“There could be things that are incongruous, but they aren't funny. Someone walking down the sidewalk and being hit by a car is incongruous, but not funny,” Martin explained.

46 years ago today, NASA’s Voyager 1 probe arrived at Saturn and beamed back the first images ever taken of its rings. It arrived at our solar system’s second-largest planet via a gravitational assist trajectory at Jupiter which was replicated with Voyager 2. On November 12th, when the space probe came within 77,000 miles of Saturn’s cloud-tops, the space probe’s cameras detected complex structures in the rings of Saturn, and its remote sensing instruments studied the atmospheres of Saturn and its giant moon Titan. READ what it discovered… (1980)
Voyager 1 found that about 7% of the volume of Saturn’s upper atmosphere is helium (compared with 11% of Jupiter’s atmosphere), while almost all the rest is hydrogen. Since Saturn’s internal helium abundance was expected to be the same as Jupiter’s and the Sun’s, the lower abundance of helium in the upper atmosphere may imply that the heavier helium may be slowly sinking through Saturn’s hydrogen; that might explain the excess heat that Saturn radiates over energy it receives from the Sun.
Winds blow at high speeds on Saturn. Near the equator, the Voyagers measured winds about 500 m/s (1,100 mph). The wind blows mostly in an easterly direction. Voyager measured the rotation of Saturn (the length of a day) at 10 hours, 39 minutes, 24 seconds, and identified polar aurorae, and aurora-like ultraviolet emissions at middle latitudes. These remain a puzzle to this day, since bombardment by electrons and ions, known to cause auroras on Earth, occurs only at the high latitudes.

Artist Sally J. Han is an exacting painter with a meticulous eye. Her detailed, colorful works depict some of life’s most ordinary moments—scrolling on a phone, peeling fruit—yet are juxtaposed with surrealist elements. Han often does this through scale. In Satellite of Love , for instance, a diminutive figure wearing a hanbok sits on a rock gazing up at an impossibly large moon that takes over the composition. It’s something we’d imagine many of us doing; however, in Han’s hands, it takes on a fantastical feel that invites many interpretations.
Han has a multicultural background, and art has served as a bridge between cultures. “From an early age, I thought of drawing as a form of communication,” she tells My Modern Met. “Having grown up in South Korea and China, and later moving to the U.S., I sometimes relied on simple sketches to express myself when I wasn’t yet familiar with the language of each country. I had always enjoyed drawing as a child, but living in different countries made it feel less like a talent and more like my own familiar way of expressing myself.”
We follow the same figure throughout Han’s work. Like the artist, the figure exists in different landscapes, including a desert sunset, a verdant tropical garden, and on a large porch with a yard. Carefully rendered elements dot the composition, like animals, tipped-over soda cans, and a pair of eyeglasses held loosely in a hand. Individually, the common objects aren’t anything special. But in Han’s visual language, they become layered and lyrical, touching on ideas of tradition and our own mythology, and ultimately shaped by our own analysis.
“I find that the familiarity and comfort of everyday life can often feel surprisingly new when viewed from a different perspective,” she explains. “I think what I enjoy most is discovering those moments.” Cultures different from her own have always fascinated her. “But what I find even more interesting is the sense of connection we can share despite our differences. I’ve always been drawn to the human side of things, and I think that naturally finds its way into my paintings.”
Han recently concluded a solo exhibition titled Gazing at Lee Art Consulting in Seoul. She’s currently working on paintings that will debut in spring 2027 at Dan Yoshii in New York City.

Despite painting himself around 35 times, there is only one confirmed photographic portrait of Vincent van Gogh that clearly shows his face. Taken in 1873, when the artist was 19 years old, the photograph captures a young Van Gogh staring unsmilingly into the camera, as was common for portrait photography at the time.
Around the time the photograph was taken, Van Gogh was working in the art trade. It would still be several years before he decided to become an artist and began creating the paintings he is known for today.
Photo: Jacobus Marinus Wilhelmus de Louw via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
Over the years, several other photographs have been associated with Van Gogh, although most have never been authenticated. One image was believed for decades to show a 13-year-old Vincent. In 2018, however, researchers determined that the boy was actually his younger brother, Theo van Gogh, who was photographed in Brussels at age 15 in 1873.
Photo: Ernest Ladrey via Wikimedia Commons (Public domain)
The mistake is understandable. The brothers shared similar features, and the photograph had been accepted as an image of Vincent for more than 60 years. Once it was correctly identified, the 1873 portrait of 19-year-old Vincent once again became his only known photographic portrait.

Sometimes referred to as a photograph of “Brussels clergymen,” the image has never been authenticated as a portrait of the artist. The Canadian photographer’s information printed on the photograph also makes the identification unlikely, since Van Gogh never traveled outside Europe.

Combining body mass index with other measurements and tests would lead to better care and outcomes, experts say
An alternative to BMI for diagnosing obesity could prevent misdiagnosis in millions of people worldwide, according to doctors who found it more accurately distinguished healthy people from those with harmful excess body fat.
Medical experts have long considered body mass index a blunt instrument for defining obesity, leading to concerns that substantial numbers of people with excess body fat are missed while others who are healthy are wrongly diagnosed.
The new approach, which combines BMI with other body measurements and organ function tests, suggests BMI alone misses obesity in 5-9% of adults, while wrongly diagnosing the condition in as many as 3%.
“This misclassification can account for tens of millions of people, so the inaccuracy of BMI is a big problem at scale and also for individuals,” said Francisco Rubino, a professor of metabolic and bariatric surgery at King’s College London.
BMI is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in metres squared. About 1.6 billion people worldwide are classified as overweight, meaning their BMI falls between 25 and 29.9, and nearly a billion with a BMI of 30 or more are considered obese. Two-thirds of adults in the UK and more than 70% of adults in the US are overweight or obese based on BMI alone.
Rubino and his colleagues drew on health records from more than 800,000 people in the UK, US, China and Spain to test a diagnostic approach for obesity that he and other world experts proposed last year in a Lancet Commission report . They used the records to track people’s health for up to 15 years.
Under the new definition, someone with a BMI over 40 is considered obese, but doctors check people with a lower BMI for excess body fat by looking at their waist measurement.
A BMI of 30-plus with a raised waist measurement or waist-to-height ratio counts as obese, as does a BMI from 25 to 29.9 if waist measurement and waist-to-height ratio are high. In most countries, a raised waist measurement means more than 102cm (40in) for men and 88cm for women, while thresholds for a high waist-to-height ratio are about 0.57.
In a second step of the diagnosis, doctors distinguish between clinical obesity, meaning an active disease where excess body fat is already impairing organ function, and pre-clinical obesity, where the extra fat is a health risk but has yet to cause problems.

items.desc: Most dengue infections cause mild flu-like symptoms or no symptoms at all. But at least one person has died from this year’s outbreak in Florida, where health experts worry the disease will become more common in the future
items.text:
McKenzie Prillaman | Assistant Digital Editor, Science & Innovation
This year, the Florida Department of Health has recorded a staggering 524 locally acquired cases of dengue , a mosquito-borne viral disease, as of October 31. That’s the highest number recorded there since the disease returned to the state in 2009 , according to Forbes ’ John Drake. For context, only 62 locally acquired cases were documented in 2025.
Most infected people either do not show symptoms or experience only mild illness . But in early September, a Tampa-area woman named Gay Rabb Small died of dengue on her 80th birthday, after developing a tremor and going to the emergency room, per the New York Times ’ Anemona Hartocollis.
Later that month, three counties in Florida declared local emergencies over the illness, and in October, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) issued a national emergency response to dengue.
“It is very unusual to have transmission in the United States,” Eva Harris , an infectious diseases expert at the University of California, Berkeley, tells the Times . “This is so very much of an eye-opener.”
Dengue is a viral disease spread by mosquitoes, mainly the species Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus , which are both present in Florida , among other places. The disease is more common in tropical and subtropical regions , where these biting insects thrive, than in temperate climates.
Around three in four infected people are asymptomatic or have mild flu-like symptoms, such as fever, headache, nausea and rash. Muscle and joint pain is another common symptom, which is why the disease is sometimes called “breakbone fever.” Symptoms usually appear within two weeks of being bitten by an infected mosquito and clear up after a week or two.
However, one in four dengue cases becomes severe. Those symptoms include extreme abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing and blood in vomit or stool, and anyone experiencing them should seek medical care. These signs often appear after the fever goes away, and people who have previously been infected are at a greater risk of severe dengue.
Individuals who recover from dengue can continue feeling fatigued for several weeks.
Although dengue vaccines exist , none are currently approved for use in the United States. They’re authorized in nations where the disease is more common, such as Argentina, Brazil, Indonesia and Thailand.

A woman has had her faith in humanity restored after neighbors arrived on paddleboards to rescue her and her son during recent flooding in Florida.
Emergency services were unable to reach her, the 911 operator said, as Brittany Grant and her son sat on their kitchen counter while floodwaters rose higher and higher above their floor.
Brevard County was recently hit by what weather reports say is a 1,000 year rain event, which flooded towns like Melbourne, Port Lucie, and Palm Bay where Grant lives with her son and 3 dogs.
Having had no luck with 911, Grant turned to Facebook asking for help. Seeing the social media SOS, neighbor Stephanie Fanguy marshalled her strapping teenage sons Jonah, 15, and Lucas, 17, who immediately planned a navigational rescue.
Embarking on an inflatable paddleboard and a borrowed kayak, Jonah and Lucas reached Grant’s house and got to work getting her son Nikoa out through what appeared on social media to be the kitchen window.
Lucas tried to calm Nikoa, who told Click Orlando he struggles with anxiety, by asking him simple questions and remarking humorously at the weather.
Eventually, mother, son, and their 3 dogs—including one which took up half the paddleboard—were all brought to safety.
“The community came together and saved us,” she said . “If it wasn’t for them, I don’t know how we would have gotten out.”
“My faith in humanity has been restored,” she added, saying that other neighbors had volunteered to help as well.
Lucas and Jonah, meanwhile, had a hero’s mentality: someone needed help and they didn’t think twice.
“Because they needed help and they were in trouble and danger, so just didn’t think about it and just went to help them,” Jonah said.

In 2017 and 2018, a pair of strange landslides moved huge masses of rock and dirt in Canada’s Northwest Territories. The events occurred in the central Mackenzie Valley, and one of them even dammed a river and created a lake .
The two natural disasters are part of a new class of landslides scientists are calling “permafrost detachment slides” in a study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters in September. They may have been partially triggered by severe wildfires that occurred in 1995, which destabilized the ground and allowed the base of the permafrost to thaw. What’s more, these events may become more common as the planet continues to warm.
“It’s a very dramatic manifestation of the changing climate,” says study co-author Joseph Young , a geoscientist who conducted the work at the University of Alberta in Canada, to Matt Simon at Grist . “They’ve only started happening in the last 10, 15 years, and it’s a very drastic and abrupt change in the landscape.”

The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art has finally opened, after 17 years of work put into its creation by George Lucas and his wife, businesswoman Mellody Hobson. While it has drawn large crowds from all walks of life, its proud founders have not forgotten that for many, particularly students and low-income families, museum pricing can be high, resulting in some missing out on a lunch or a treat during a visit. As such, they’ve implemented a few measures to keep it budget-friendly for everyone.
The inspiration behind this lies in Hobson’s personal story. While today she is president and co-CEO of Ariel Investments, and a former chair of both DreamWorks and Starbucks, Hobson grew up in poverty. Her mother, a single parent of six, struggled to make ends meet, sometimes not even having enough money to pay the rent. As a result of this financial challenge, Hobson often found herself unable to afford any food as a kid on a field trip at a museum. These experiences marked her profoundly. In fact, it prompted the couple to create affordable options for all visitors to their museum, where the lobby café offers $2 grilled cheese sandwiches. These simply yet satisfying sandwiches are made with American and cheddar cheese melted together between slices of buttered Pullman bread.
“That was the directive from the founders, George and Mellody,” Katie Harel, the restaurant’s managing director, told Forbes , “who were adamant that there would be something affordable in the café for everyone. So everyone can eat something in the café for $2. Every single person.” In addition to the grilled cheese option, the museum café also offers a $3 peanut butter and jelly sandwich.
Since no museum visit is complete without a trip to the gift shop, the Lucas Museum also offers some affordable souvenirs. The on-site shop sells 25¢ pencils listed as the Mellody Pencil . Part of the First Draft Collection , the stylish pencils include cheeky markings indicating how much of the pencil it would take to write a first, second, third, and final draft. From the brink of extinction to roaming across 6,500 square miles, populations of Cantabrian brown bears have doubled in Spain over the last 20 years to 370.
Numbering as few as 140 by estimates in the early 21st century, they’re another example of Spain’s ongoing success in protecting several of the country’s endemic species.
Taking its name from the far northern Spanish region whose mountains stand as the bear’s last redoubt, Cantabrian brown bears can actually be found across the regions of Asturians, Leon, Galicia, and Palencia, in addition to Cantabria.
By restricting the movement of animals, the Iberian Peninsula’s northern mountain ranges have led to high rates of endemism in Spain and Portugal among animals such as the wolf, lynx, and bear.
Direct human persecution and the conversion of wilderness to agricultural land gradually impacted the brown bear’s numbers until they could only be found in Cantabria. Yet they clung to existence in the mountains until sufficient protections were put in place for them to gain a second wind.
A study published in 2023 bears witness to the successful survival and spread by Spain’s bears. Published in the journal Conservation Science and Practice, it found that the government’s continual protection measures and establishment of new protected areas, coupled with rural depopulation, allowed the bears to substantially recover.
Using all data available to them, the authors measured the changes in population numbers across 3 periods: from 1982 to 1992, from 1993 to 2002, and from 2003 to 2012.
While a 25% reduction in the numbers of bears was observed between the first 2 periods, this was followed by a 70% increase by the end of the 3rd period. That final period also saw their breeding ranges expand by 30%, such that Cantabria’s 2 breeding populations now overlap, having been separated for decades by an 18-24 mile series of gorges with a highway running through them.
The first 2 periods coincided with the creation of Somiedo Natural Park and Redes National Park respectively, which increased the amount of protected areas centered on the last remaining populations of brown bears 688 square kilometers. Fines for unauthorized killing of bears reached some $350,000.
Additional growth in the geographical range of 77% was observed by the authors between 2013 and 2022 in exactly the proportion and areas they predicted.

Yet as the woman, who revealed herself only as Betsy, rummaged around in that closet 4 years later, she found an oil painting of undulating hills, with soft earthen colors reminiscent of the female form, which is now known to be Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I, painted by the Mother of Modernism in 1930.
Its rediscovery has been hailed as “a once-in-a-lifetime moment, and absolutely thrilling.”
Soon to be auctioned at Christie’s where it’s expected to garner around $3 million, the story of its provenance first broke at the New York Post , who talked to Betsy about the fateful closet-cleaning
Her aunt, she said, was an “extremely intelligent” former foreign service member who had received the painting from Georgia O’Keeffe’s Manhattan art dealer in 1963 as a graduation present from her parents. At the time time it cost $3,800.

She decided to take it down so as to not draw attention to herself during similar soirées. Amid her fur coats the painting sat, even after her niece came over in 2022 to help clean out the apartment as the woman prepared to enter hospice care. It was only after her aunt passed away that Betsy followed up on the comment of the “O’Keeffe in the closet” that she found it, still in its original box marked “The Downtown Gallery, 51st St.”

More than 260 years ago, Martha Washington wrote to a friend with encouraging news about her young daughter’s health. Now, that letter has found a new home at the Library of Congress, offering a rare glimpse into the family’s private life.
Martha penned the note on September 29, 1760. Writing to Margaret Bolan Green, she provided an update on her four-year-old daughter “Patsy.”
“I have the pleasure to tell you my dear little girl is much better,” she wrote. “She has lost her fitts & fevours bout and seems to be getting well very fast.”
The Library of Congress purchased the letter for $47,500 in June during a Heritage Auctions sale, with funding from the James Madison Council’s Edwin L. Cox Legacy Trust, a permanent endowment that helps the library acquire materials. The library already had 11 of Martha’s letters, but this is the first that bears her handwriting.
“Very few of Martha Washington’s letters survive, as she appears to have destroyed most of her own private correspondence,” Elizabeth Novara , the American women’s history specialist for the library’s Manuscript Division, writes in a blog post . “Even brief documentation of her relationships with family and friends, as may be found in this letter, is important to understanding women’s lives during this time period.”
“Patsy”—whose full name was Martha Parke Custis —was one of the four children Martha had with her first husband, Daniel Parke Custis . The two had been married for just seven years when Custis died from a sudden illness in July 1757, at the age of 45. Two years later, at age 27, the widowed Martha married George Washington. Together, they raised the two surviving children from Martha’s first marriage, Patsy and John “Jacky” Parke Custis . (The other two, Daniel Parke Custis and Frances Parke Custis, died while their father was still alive.).
Historians believe that William Costin , a prominent member of Washington, D.C.’s free Black community, was likely Martha Washington’s grandson —the child of her son from her first marriage, Jacky, and an enslaved woman.
Martha wrote the letter after George Washington had served as commander of the Virginia Regiment during the French and Indian War but before he had become the nation’s first president . Historians now suspect that Patsy’s “fitts & fevours” were symptoms of epilepsy , a neurological disorder caused by abnormal bursts of electrical activity in the brain. Droughts and wildfires in the summer were a wake-up call, and winter flooding could leave Wales' food supply vulnerable, an expert has warned.
The country currently imports the vast majority of its fruit and vegetables, with only 6% of those served in its schools grown in Wales.
It is dependent on produce from parts of the world prone to droughts and fires, according to co-founder of an organisation aiming to address this.
Duncan Fisher is behind Our Food Trust , external , which wants to build 100 farms, producing fruit and vegetables in Wales for local markets.

Food security has become a hot topic , with Defence Secretary Wes Streeting saying in October people should have water, tinned goods, baby food, torches and mobile phone charging packs ready in case of emergency.

He said: "There's no storage, it's a just-in-time system so the food is stored in lorries moving across motorways.

Researchers discover a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread
A molecular signal in the blood helps identify microscopic changes that precede development of ovarian cancer, researchers have found, ⁠a potential diagnostic breakthrough for a disease often ⁠discovered after it has already spread.
For decades, ​efforts to detect ovarian cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumors, the researchers noted in their report published on Tuesday in Nature Medicine.
“We asked a fundamentally different question: What if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” study leader Rajan Gogna of the Hoag Family Cancer Institute in ⁠Newport Beach, California, said in a statement.
Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The precancerous lesions are known as serous tubal intraepithelial carcinoma.
The new study found that women with this precursor condition have elevated blood levels of an RNA molecule called Tu-Stroma.
When researchers measured Tu-Stroma in blood, they detected STIC in 92.3% of affected women ⁠and correctly identified 98.2% of healthy women.
In women with genetic risk factors for ovarian cancer, approximately 72% of positive results would be accurate, while negative results would be correct nearly 100% of the time, they reported.
“For women at high risk, this ​could transform how we approach prevention,” co-author Dr Esha Madan, also of Hoag, said in a statement.
Many such women ‌face difficult decisions about preventive surgery to remove their fallopian tubes ‌and ovaries.
“Today, decisions about preventive surgery are largely guided by inherited risk, without knowing whether precancerous lesions are actually present,” Madan said. “Our discovery could eventually provide that missing biological information.”

Bafta-winning actors Toby Jones and Emily Watson have finished work on a film about the scientist behind Britain's first spacecraft to land on Mars, which got "lost".
Mars Express, directed by Mackenzie Crook, will see Jones play Colin Pillinger while Watson is his wife Judith.
The couple began developing the unmanned Beagle 2 probe to search for life on Mars while Pillinger was a professor of planetary sciences at the Open University in Milton Keynes. The probe went out of contact upon landing in December 2003, until it was finally spotted in 2015, after Pillinger died.
Crook said: "It's a complete honour to be telling the extraordinary story... for my first feature film as director."
Pillinger died believing that Beagle 2 had not safely landed on Mars
Pillinger, originally from Kingswood near Bristol, became a familiar face in the 1990s as he sought public support and funding for the ambitious mission, enlisting celebrities and pop stars to help promote it.
Beagle 2 was launched into space on board the European Space Agency's Mars Express orbiter.
His Beagle 2 lander was due to touch down on 25 December 2003, but failed to send a signal confirming it had landed safely.
The mission was considered a failure for years, however, in January 2015 images taken by US space agency Nasa showed the lander had reached the surface safely.
Pillinger died eight months earlier following a brain haemorrhage.
Mars Express is the first feature-length film to be directed by actor Mackenzie Crook
The director added: "Joe Bone's beautiful script has made it easy to attract some of the best names in the business to join our brilliantly creative team and I'm thrilled to be working once again with my friend Toby Jones."
Crook, known for his roles in The Office and Pirates of the Caribbean, previously worked with Jones on Detectorists , the BBC's Bafta-winning comedy he wrote, directed and starred in.
He also starred in Small Prophets, a comedy which made its debut on BBC Two and the BBC iPlayer in February.
The film is expected to be released in 2027.

“He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail.” That’s how one rescuer in Kentucky described the moment he spotted 6-year-old Roman Heilman, a boy with autism missing for 3 days.
Jacob Mullins, a member of a local horse trailriding group, told the Lexington Herald Leader that he was only about a half-mile from Heilman’s home when he suddenly climbed out of a bush followed by a small dog, and and sang “Old McDonald.”
Heilman then grabbed onto the leg of the lead rescuer and didn’t want to let go.
He had been reported missing in the late afternoon on Sunday, November 1st, and the volunteers had been out since first light on Tuesday, looking around the wooded and mountainous area for hours, covering some 14 miles.
1 of 10 members of a horse trailriding group who live either side of the Kentucky-West Virginia state line, Jacob Mullins told the Lexington Herald Leader about the moment that the hunters became the hunted.
“We found him probably about a mile and a half from his house. He came out of the bushes saying ‘E-I-E-I-O horsey.’ He just walked right out of the bushes onto a horse trail,” Mullins remembered.
“He was naked, and he was scratched, and he had a little dog with him. He ate a banana and drank some water and then we brought him off the hill.”
Roman is autistic, and when it was reported to police that he had wandered away from his house into the woods, “hundreds” volunteered to aid in the search. This included other teams on horseback, drones, but also motor vehicles, which Mullins thought perhaps had scared the boy from being found earlier.
Rescue authorities had received information on Sunday that the child had removed his clothing at some point, making the situation even more concerning. Indeed, he would have spent two frigid nights in the woods.
Travis Hughes, Director of Lawrence County Emergency Management, put out a heartfelt statement following the rescue on Facebook, in which he said he had “never been more proud” of the community.

On October 31, four NASA crewmembers returned from “Mars.” Not the actual Red Planet, of course, but a 3D-printed Mars habitat in Houston where the three men and one woman lived for 378 days.
Now, the Mars analog astronauts— Ross Elder , Ellen Ellis , James Spicer and Matthew Montgomery —have started telling the world what took place after they disappeared into NASA’s Mars Dune Alpha habitat at the Johnson Space Center on October 19, 2025, for the agency’s second Crew Health and Performance Exploration Analog (CHAPEA) mission.
The mission aimed to test the kinds of physical and mental conditions that a team of Mars explorers would endure on the Red Planet, including long-term isolation, disrupted communication with people on Earth and food cultivation. The habitat includes both a base and a mock outdoor environment , so the crew could practice Marswalks.
“For more than a year, they have lived in an isolated environment, conducting critical research and helping us better understand what it will take to send humans to Mars,” Vanessa Wyche , director of NASA’s Johnson Space Center, said during a livestream , just before the crew emerged. “Inside just 1,700 square feet, they managed to live with limited resources. After the speech, NASA astronaut Jack Hathaway , who had just completed a mission at the International Space Station, knocked on the door to the Mars habitat, called out “trick or treat” and opened it to reveal the crew’s smiling faces. Since then, the analog astronauts have been participating in post-mission evaluations and debriefs that, along with the data collected during their year in the simulated environment, will help inform future missions to Mars and those closer to home, per a NASA statement .

items.title: What Seeded Life on Earth? New Research Challenges the Longstanding Theory That Comets Brought the Ingredients to Our Planet
items.desc: Computer simulations suggest comets carrying a key precursor to many of life's building blocks would have rarely—if ever—successfully reached Earth's surface. And even if they did, only specific landing conditions would have allowed the precursor molecule to drive biologically relevant reactions
items.text:
The question of how life started on Earth has proven to be almost as enigmatic as finding organisms on alien worlds. A longstanding theory posits that comets delivered the molecular ingredients that kickstarted life when they smacked into our planet during its youth. But new research suggests that this popular scenario is extremely unlikely.
In a study published October 28 in the journal Scientific Reports , researchers ran computer simulations of the celestial mail service and found that successful deliveries would have been rare, if not impossible. While the findings reorient discussions on the origin of life on Earth, they also posit a slightly more likely place where comets could’ve brought biologically useful organic molecules: our next-door neighbor, Mars.
The team investigated the potential delivery of hydrogen cyanide (HCN), a molecule with hydrogen, carbon and nitrogen, that would’ve been made with leftovers from the solar system’s formation 4.6 billion years ago . It has been detected on many comets and can be a precursor for many of life’s essential building blocks, including lipids , sugars and nucleotides . That’s because the carbon-containing, or organic, molecule has an extremely strong chemical bond that can drive subsequent reactions. The bond also makes it very stable, and thus more likely than other organics to survive an impact.
“So, if things look bad for hydrogen cyanide, then we think it’s going to be much harder for other, more complicated molecules that are more likely to be broken down during these impacts,” lead author Richard Anslow , a planetary scientist who conducted the research at the University of Cambridge in England, tells Science News ’ Skyler Ware.
Comets , sometimes dubbed “dirty snowballs,” are masses of frozen gases, rock and dust located primarily in the outer solar system. When their orbit brings them closer to the sun, their materials get heated up and form a glowing head, as well as a tail that streaks across the sky.
And things did indeed look bad. Anslow and colleagues analyzed comet impact simulations, interactions between the atmosphere and comets, and models of the origin and evolution of comets. They found that comets likely wouldn’t have been able to supply enough HCN needed to seed life on Earth.

Mexico City is a city of flowers. Around the Day of the Dead, the main avenues are painted orange with thousands upon thousands of marigolds, which later make way for red poinsettias as Christmas time arrives. And come spring, the jacaranda trees cover the ground with lilac-hued blooms. As such, the Mexican capital is the perfect spot for artist Cj Hendry to open a pop-up of her Flower Shop, offering her colorful plush blooms that blend art, design, and collectibles.
From Nov. 21 to 29, Cj Hendry’s Flower Shop will operate in the bustling Roma Norte neighborhood. The pop-up will feature a carefully curated collection of plush flowers, including a special selection of blooms that reflects the personality and energy of the host city. The organizers say the flowers will be priced at 150 pesos each (about $8). With every purchase of nine flowers, guests will receive a complimentary 10th one.
The Mexico City pop-up is part of a larger Flower Shop international tour, following the opening of permanent Flower Markets in New York and Hong Kong. After this stop, the plush blooms will make their way to Miami, Denver, London, Melbourne, Sydney, Brisbane, and Perth.
“Flower Market began as an effort to unite communities around a universally shared joy: flowers,” says Hendry via a statement. “By expanding into Flower Shop, the goal was to share that experience globally, allowing people across various cities to engage with and gather these tactile creations. Each locale possesses a distinct atmosphere, and I am thrilled that every temporary installation will feature unique floral variations, distinctive surprises, and a tailored narrative.”
The Mexico City pop-up will be located at Mérida 87, Roma Norte, taking place Nov. 21-29 and open every day between 10 a.m. and 6 p.m. There is also no need to go on the very first day of the event. According to the organizers, the flowers will be restocked every single day.

“The blast blasted blubber beyond all believable bounds.”
TV newsman Paul Linnman delivered that line from an Oregon beach in 1970. Fifty-six years later, people still repeat it to him everywhere he goes.
“It is just such a ridiculous, incredible, amazing, very human story,” director Winslow Crane-Murdoch told GNN.
That story is the subject of Oh Whale! , the latest film in GNN’s JoyDrops series.
On November 12, 1970, a massive dead whale washed ashore near Florence, Oregon. The highway department decided the best way to get rid of it was dynamite.
“That was about as bad of an idea as you can imagine it to be,” Crane-Murdoch said. A young Portland newscaster named Paul Linnman was sent to cover it, along with a cameraman named Doug Brazil. When the blast rained blubber across the beach, they ran for their lives. Their report “ended up defining his entire career and becoming one of the most viral news stories of all time.”
Crane-Murdoch, who moved to Oregon in 2017, first saw the footage on YouTube a few years later, when the station released a remastered version for the 50th anniversary. “I was quite literally blown away, to use a bad pun that we use many times in the film,” he said.
As he dug in, he found a deeper story. For years, Linnman resented being remembered for the whale over everything else he reported. Over time, he came to accept it. Oh Whale! follows that journey.
The film is being released with The New Yorker and Switchboard Magazine .
The clip has gone viral again and again for 56 years. First people requested film reels, then VHS tapes. It became one of the first email attachments and early blog videos, and then a YouTube hit.

items.text:
An 81-year-old Englishman grew up wondering who his real father was. What he didn’t know was that an entire family tree in Canada was wondering who and where he was.
After being divided by a world war, an ocean, and 8 decades, Rodney Anderson has finally found his long lost relatives with the help of a simple DNA test, and a persistent, curious niece.
“I thought ‘This is a wind up.’ It has to be,” Anderson said, sharing with CBC News the moment he learned of his true origins.
“But it wasn’t. You can’t believe what a shock it is to get that knowledge.”
Anderson’s mother had a child with a visiting Canadian soldier during the Second World War, a secret that his mother and grandmother never shared with him.
He grew up with no knowledge or explanation of his father’s origins whatsoever because of the stigma attached at the time to these out-of-wedlock births, even though they came about during a period of immense crisis and uncertainty about the future.
Canadian Bethany Allen began searching in 2008 for this mystery uncle of hers after discovering in divorce papers that her grandfather, Charles Blakney, had had a child with a woman in the UK in 1944.
He had first sailed off to war in 1942, leaving behind a wife and daughter in New Brunswick. Blakney served as a motor and driver mechanic with the New Brunswick Rangers and returned home in 1945, the same year that Rodney Anderson was born in Farnham to his mother Yvonne. Rumors of his affair overseas remained in the family long after the guns fell silent in Europe.
“My mother [Rodney’s half-sister] had always wanted to know that [Anderson] had a good life and was happy,” Bethany Allen told CBC News.

Dr. King’s Final Draft of ‘I have a dream’ Appears After 60 Years
(totally alternative approach) Incredible Discovery of King’s Own ‘I have a dream’ Draft Chills Readers with its Insights
A penned draft of the famous ‘I have a Dream’ speech, written by Martin Luther King Jr. the morning of the famous event on the Lincoln Memorial, has resurfaced after 6 decades.
Unlike any other examples of his longhand writing ever found, the draft’s copious revisions tell of a man who understood the gravity of what he was preparing to say.
The New York Times reports that King’s own draft of the speech had been presumed lost. Those which are known had all been drafted and or typed up by his aides.
Now, Xernona Clayton, the widow of King’s former aide Edward Clayton, has revealed to the nation in its 250th year that she had found the handwritten draft in her deceased husband’s desk drawer in the 1990s, but only recently decided to put it up for auction at Christie’s for the benefit of several charities, including the King Center in Atlanta.
She found it one day in an envelope marked “Speech,” and though she recognized the words immediately, it never occurred to her that it might have been written by the speaker himself.
“This is the most important manuscript I’ve ever had the honor to handle,” Peter Klarnet, Christie’s manuscript specialist, told the Times, adding that he couldn’t imagine getting his hands on anything better that he “wouldn’t have to steal out of the National Archives.”
This relic of American oratory consists of 7 yellow pages covered in blue ink. Words, and sometimes whole paragraphs are crossed out. In some cases, a word was crossed out to be replaced by another word which was also crossed out.
It captures the mood in the Washington hotel where Dr. King was working on the speech with his colleagues who had spent days exploring various themes and directions it might take. He had been told to limit the speech to 5 minutes—pressure—all while knowing that President John Kennedy had only 2 months prior sent the proposed Civil Rights Act to Congress where it had not yet been voted on—more pressure.

The draft is very close to the typed document which King set before the microphones, yet it’s unclear whether the large crossed out sections—which have already undergone digital examination—will reveal new insights into King’s ideas, or mood

“It was like looking for a needle in a haystack.”
That’s how Professor Daniel Mège described the discovery of trace volcanic gases on Mars that could be key to finding life on the Red Planet.
The discovery centers around hydrogen chloride gas seeping out through volcanic rifts—something of a “smoking gun” that suggests Mars is not geologically dead, but merely sleeping.
These gases hint at magma, which, when coming into contact with groundwater can produce warm habitable niches for organisms beneath the Red Planet’s surface.
“If hydrothermal systems are active, they could contain the ingredients and energy needed for microorganisms to develop, and shield microorganisms from the hostile and changing environment above the surface,” one of the scientists behind the discovery hypothesized.
Mars is studded with the largest volcanoes in the solar system, and fresh fissures on the surface of one of the largest, called Alba Mons, hint at volcanically active spots under the surface.
Detected by a European Space Agency (ESA) orbiter, an international research team believes that the release of hydrogen chloride from these fissures comes from hot magma beneath the surface.
The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) first reported hydrogen chloride gas in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. The gas is commonly found escaping from magmatic vents on Earth, leading researchers to wonder whether the same was happening on Mars.
Evidence for active volcanism on Mars has always been extremely elusive, yet enough has been identified in the form of geologically-recent lava flows and “marsquakes” over the last 50 years, so as never to rule it out.
Now again, researchers noticed spikes of hydrogen chloride where they shouldn’t have been, and during an odd season in the northern hemisphere of Mars.
Study co-leader Professor Daniel Mège, from the Space Research Center of the Polish Academy of Sciences, said the gas varies seasonally on Mars, reaching its maximum in the northern winter, then mostly disappearing in the summer.
But there was one exception to the pattern, always in the same season and at the same place: above volcanic fissures on the flanks of the Alba Mons volcano, in early summer.
